articles.title: Designing AI developer tools that feel made for engineers
articles.seoTitle: Designing UX for AI Developer Tools · Mihai Boboc
articles.description: Lessons from redesigning Angen AI: why AI coding tools should mirror the IDE, put the task first, separate planning from coding and keep context in view.
articles.text:
AI coding tools are multiplying, and a lot of them look the same: a chat box, a stream of answers, and code somewhere underneath. When I redesigned Angen AI, a tool that turns natural-language tasks into production-ready code, the product already worked. It just felt like a generic chat app, and developers don’t live in chat apps. They live in their editors.

Here is what I learned about designing for that audience.

## Start from the tools they already use

Before drawing anything, I reviewed tools like GitHub Copilot and Cursor and gathered feedback from developers. The pattern was clear: developers trust interfaces that behave like the environments they already know. They don’t want to learn a new mental model just to ask for code.

So the new layout mirrors a modern IDE: three panels, with navigation on the left, the work in the middle and context on the right. Nothing about it is surprising, and that is the point. Familiar structure frees attention for the actual task.

## Structure over novelty

AI products are tempted to show off. Animated responses, clever empty states, a personality. For developer tools, I think the opposite works better. The interface should get out of the way and make the state of the work obvious.

In Angen AI, navigation used to mix tools, resources and settings in one list. Separating them made it clear where you are and what you can do next, which matters more than any visual flourish.

## Make the task the centre of the screen

A chat thread is organised by time. Real work is organised by tasks. The redesigned workbench is task-first: each task has its own space, and tabs keep several of them open at once, so switching between them no longer breaks focus.

## Separate planning from doing

One of the most useful changes was splitting the work into two modes: Plan and Code. Planning is where you and the AI agree on what should happen. Coding is where it happens. Keeping them apart gives developers a moment to check the approach before any code is written, and makes it easier to trust what comes out.

## Keep context next to the work

Files and knowledge used to sit apart from the task, so developers had to go looking for what the AI was working with. A context panel beside the workbench keeps that information in view. When people can see what the AI sees, its answers are easier to judge.

## Design for long sessions

Developers spend hours in these tools, often in the dark. The design system for Angen AI came with light and dark themes from the start, not as an afterthought.

## The takeaway

Designing AI tools for developers is less about the AI and more about the workflow around it. Respect the patterns developers already rely on, make the task the centre of the screen, and keep people in control of what the AI does. That is how a functional prototype becomes a tool that feels made for engineers.

If you’re building an AI product for developers and want a second pair of eyes, I’d be happy to talk.

articles.title: Building trust in a peer-to-peer marketplace
articles.seoTitle: Building Trust in Peer-to-Peer Marketplaces · Mihai Boboc
articles.description: How Lendit makes renting from a stranger feel safe: lead with the person, ask before you charge, let AI help but keep people in charge, and stay consistent.
articles.text:
A marketplace where strangers rent things to each other only works if both sides trust what they see. That was the core design problem behind Lendit, the app that lets neighbours rent everyday things to each other: drills, ladders, cameras.

People already borrow from friends, put projects off, or buy a tool they’ll use once. Asking them to lend their own things to someone they’ve never met is a big step. Here is how design helped make it feel smaller.

## Lead with the person, not the product

On most marketplaces the item comes first. On Lendit, every card leads with the lender’s face, name and distance. You are not renting from a platform; you are borrowing from someone who lives a few streets away.

We tested this early. A review of the item card compared versions, and the one that led with the person, with ratings rounded to whole stars, was the clear choice. That hierarchy now anchors every listing.

## Ask before you charge

Money is where trust breaks first. On Lendit a booking starts as a request, and nothing is charged until the lender accepts. Borrowers never pay for something that might not happen, and lenders stay in control of who uses their things.

## Let AI help, but keep people in charge

Creating a listing is work, and work stops people from lending. AI Quick Listing drafts a listing from a few photos, but the lender approves it before it goes live. The AI saves time; the person keeps the final say. That balance matters in any product where trust is the currency.

## Make the whole product feel reliable

Consistency is a quiet form of trust. As the only designer working with four developers, I built a design system the team ships from, with 100+ components and 500+ variables. When every screen behaves the same way, people stop wondering whether the product is going to surprise them.

## Build trust offline too

A neighbourhood product also has to be visible in the neighbourhood. For Lendit I designed A5 leaflets with local QR codes and real photos of real handovers, and an event gazebo for community street festivals. Seeing the brand on the street makes the app feel less like a stranger.

## The takeaway

Trust in a peer-to-peer marketplace is designed one decision at a time: who appears first on a card, when money moves, who has the final word, and how consistent the experience feels. Lendit is live and has passed 500 users, and testing hasn’t stopped.

If you’re designing a marketplace and want to talk about trust, I’d be glad to help.
